entities.name: Spanish House of Bourbon
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Spanish House of Bourbon, established when Philip V (grandson of Louis XIV of France) was recognized as King of Spain after the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714), has ruled Spain — with interruptions — from 1700 to the present day, making it the world's longest-continuously ruling Bourbon line and one of Europe's oldest surviving dynasties. The war that created the dynasty (the War of Spanish Succession) was one of the century's most destructive conflicts, reshaping the European balance of power: Spain lost its Italian territories (Naples, Milan, Sardinia) and the Spanish Netherlands to Austria, and gave Britain Gibraltar (retained to the present).

The Spanish Bourbons' 18th-century Bourbon Reforms — modeled on French administrative centralization — reorganized Spain's American empire: intendancies replaced venal offices, monopoly trading companies were established, free trade within the empire (1778) increased commerce, and the military was professionalized. These reforms increased revenue dramatically but also fueled resentment in the Americas that contributed to independence movements (1810-1825). Charles III (r. 1759-1788) was the dynasty's Enlightenment peak — expelling the Jesuits (1767), reforming agriculture, and modernizing Madrid.

The dynasty survived Napoleon's 1808 invasion (which placed Joseph Bonaparte on the throne), the 1812 Constitution of Cádiz (Spain's first), the loss of American colonies (1810-1825), civil wars, and republican periods. Juan Carlos I (r. 1975-2014) — restored by Franco to transition Spain to democracy after his 1975 death — led Spain's transition from dictatorship to democracy and oversaw Spain's 1986 European Union entry. His son Felipe VI (b. 1968, r. 2014-present) is the current king, making the Spanish Bourbons Europe's most active surviving royal dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Spanish House of Bourbon — ruling Spain for 300+ years, losing the Americas (1825) while modernizing with Enlightenment reforms, surviving Napoleon's invasion, and leading Spain's democratic transition (1975) — is Europe's most continuously resilient royal dynasty and the only Bourbon line ruling its original kingdom today.
